entry: Pungent fruit of plants of the genus *Capsicum*. Chili peppers, also spelled chile or chilli, belong to the nightshade family [[Solanaceae]] and are used as a [[Spice|spice]] in many cuisines. Their heat comes from [[Capsaicin|capsaicin]] and related capsaicinoids. Chili peppers originated in Central or South America and were first cultivated in Mexico. European explorers brought them to the Old World in the late 15th century as part of the [[Columbian exchange]]. Diego Álvarez Chanca, who accompanied [[Christopher Columbus]] on his second voyage in 1493, published the first European account of their medicinal uses in 1494. Columbus's crew called the fruits "peppers" because they were pungent like [[Black pepper|black pepper]]. By 1569 they had reached the Balkans, where they were processed into [[Paprika|paprika]]. Portuguese and Spanish traders probably introduced them to Africa and Asia in the 16th century, including [[Sri Lanka]]. Global production reached approximately 37 million metric tons in 2022, led by China with about 45% of output.

Cartilaginous fish in the order Chimaeriformes. Chimaeras, also called ghost sharks or ratfish, are soft-bodied, shark-like fish with bulky heads and long, tapered tails, reaching up to 150 cm (4.9 ft). Like other members of the class [[Chondrichthyes]], their skeletons are entirely [[Cartilage|cartilaginous]]. Their closest living relatives are [[Shark|sharks]] and rays, from which their last common ancestor diverged nearly 400 million years ago. The group was once diverse and abundant, and fossils from the [[Carboniferous]] period, over 300 million years ago, document chimaeroid forms. Living species, apart from plough-nose chimaeras, are largely confined to deep water, some below 2,000 m (6,600 ft). Instead of sharks' replaceable teeth, they have six permanent tooth-plates that form a beaklike crushing mechanism, comparable to the incisors of [[Rodent|rodents]]. Some chimaeras have a [[Venom|venomous]] spine on the front of the dorsal fin.

Monstrous fire-breathing hybrid creature in [[Greek mythology]]. Typically depicted as a [[Lion|lion]] with a [[Goat|goat]]'s head protruding from its back and a tail ending in a [[Snake|snake]]'s head, it was said to come from Lycia in Asia Minor. It was the offspring of Typhon and Echidna and a sibling of [[Cerberus]]. [[Homer]] described it in the [[Iliad]] as a "bane to many men", and the hero Bellerophon, riding the winged [[Pegasus]], killed it. The term now describes any mythical or fictional creature with parts taken from various animals.

Architectural ventilation structure of masonry, clay, or metal, for hot exhaust gases and smoke. Chimneys are built as near vertical as possible so that rising gases draw air into [[Combustion|combustion]] through the stack effect. The space inside is called the flue. Chimneys carry gases from a [[Stove|stove]], [[Fireplace|fireplace]], boiler, or furnace away from living areas. Domestic chimneys first appeared in large dwellings in northern Europe in the 12th century, and the earliest surviving English example, at the keep of [[Castle|Conisbrough Castle]] in [[Yorkshire]], dates from 1185. Chimneys became common in ordinary houses only in the 16th and 17th centuries. In the 18th and 19th centuries, the extraction of [[Lead|lead]] from ore produced toxic fumes, and long near-horizontal chimneys in northern England, often more than 3 km (2 mi) long, carried them to a remote vertical stack.

Political grouping of the Chimú culture on the northern coast of Peru. The Chimú culture arose about 900 CE, succeeding the [[Moche culture]], and developed on a desert strip where rivers carved fertile valleys suited to irrigation. Chimor was the largest kingdom of the Late Intermediate Period, encompassing 1,000 km (620 mi) of coastline. Its capital, Chan Chan, was founded, according to legend, by Taycanamo. Irrigation [[Canal|canals]] extended up to 80 km, and the Chimú are known for distinctive monochromatic [[Pottery|pottery]], usually with a shiny black finish, and for metalwork in [[Gold|gold]] and [[Silver|silver]]. The Chimú worshipped the [[Moon]] and traded Spondylus shells from the coast of present-day Ecuador. The [[Inca Empire]] conquered Chimor around 1470, 50 years before the Spanish arrived in the region.

Medium-sized great ape species of equatorial Africa. Chimpanzees live in forests and savannas, and four subspecies are confirmed. They share the genus *Pan* with the [[Bonobo]], and fossil and DNA evidence show that the two species are the closest living relatives of [[Human|humans]]. Chimpanzees eat mainly fruit, but also insects, and will hunt smaller monkeys. Nearly all populations use tools, such as modified sticks, for hunting and for obtaining [[Honey]], [[Termite|termites]], and [[Ant|ants]]. Groups can number more than 200 members, with a male-dominated hierarchy in which disputes are generally settled without violence. The species is listed as [[Endangered species|endangered]] on the IUCN Red List, with habitat loss, poaching, and disease as the main threats. Some hundreds have been kept in laboratories, mainly in the United States. Attempts to teach them sign language have been made, but academics such as [[Noam Chomsky]] have questioned whether they can acquire language.

National space agency of [[China|the People's Republic of China]]. Founded in 1993 and headquartered in Haidian, Beijing, the agency manages China's civil space programs and international space cooperation. It is a national bureau under the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. Its Chang'e program made China the first space agency to land on the [[Far side of the Moon|far side of the Moon]], with Chang'e 4, and returned lunar material with Chang'e 5 and 6. Tianwen-1 made China the second agency to land a rover on Mars. Construction of the [[Tiangong space station]] began in 2021 and was completed in late 2022. Since the Wolf Amendment of 2011, Congress has required [[NASA]] to exclude cooperation with the agency, although this has been periodically overcome.

1974 American neo-noir mystery film directed by [[Roman Polanski]]. Written by Robert Towne, *Chinatown* stars [[Jack Nicholson]] and [[Faye Dunaway]]. Its story is inspired by the California water wars, in which Los Angeles secured water rights in the Owens Valley. It was Polanski's last film made in the [[United States]]. The film received 11 nominations at the [[Academy Awards]], winning for Towne's screenplay. It was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]] in 1991.

Genus of two species of crepuscular [[Rodent|rodents]] native to the [[Andes]] of [[South America]]. The short-tailed *Chinchilla chinchilla* and the long-tailed *C. lanigera* live in colonies called [[Herd|herds]] at elevations up to 4,270 m (14,000 ft). Chinchillas have around 20,000 hairs per square centimeter, the densest fur of any extant terrestrial mammal. After being hunted for their soft fur, they had become rare by the end of the 19th century. Wild colonies are now known only in [[Chile]]. Most chinchillas used by the [[Fur|fur]] industry are farm-raised, and domestic chinchillas descended from *C. lanigera* are kept as pets.

Armed conflict in China from 1927 to 1949 between the government of the [[Republic of China (1912–1949)|Republic of China]], led by the [[Kuomintang]], and the [[Chinese Communist Party]]. In 1926 and 1927 the two parties, allied in the First United Front, conducted the Northern Expedition against regional warlords. War broke out between them on August 1, 1927. From 1937 to 1945 they fought the Japanese invasion together during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]], though armed clashes continued. After Japan's defeat, the [[Mao Zedong|Communists under Mao Zedong]] gained the upper hand and proclaimed the People's Republic of China in October 1949. The [[Chiang Kai-shek|Nationalist government]] retreated to [[Taiwan]] in December 1949. The two sides have since faced each other across the [[Taiwan Strait]], and no armistice or peace treaty has been signed.

Sole governing party of the People's Republic of China. Founded in 1921, the party won the [[Chinese Civil War]] against the [[Kuomintang]] and proclaimed the People's Republic in October 1949 under the chairmanship of [[Mao Zedong]]. Mao remained its most influential member until 1976. [[Deng Xiaoping]] then directed the party toward reform and opening up in the 1980s. [[Xi Jinping]] has led the party since 2012. As of 2025, the party had more than 101 million members, the second-largest political party by membership in the world. Supporters credit its reforms with lifting over 800 million people out of extreme poverty since 1978. Critics point to the 1989 military crackdown on pro-democracy protests and argue that the party has tightened political control and censorship.

Traditional holiday in Chinese culture, also called the Spring Festival. It marks the start of the year on the lunisolar [[Chinese calendar]], falling on the new moon between January 21 and February 20. In more than 96 percent of years, it falls on the new moon closest to the beginning of [[Spring (season)|spring]]. The celebration runs from New Year's Eve to the Lantern Festival on the 15th day. Families hold a reunion dinner, clean their homes to sweep away ill fortune, display red paper-cuts and couplets, set off [[Fireworks|firecrackers]], and give money in red envelopes. The holiday is also widely observed in [[Singapore]], [[Malaysia]], the [[Philippines]], and [[Thailand]], and it has influenced Lunar New Year celebrations in Korea, Vietnam, and Tibet.

Architectural style of China, influential across [[East Asia]]. Chinese architecture uses a timber-frame system whose structural principles have remained largely unchanged since the early ancient era, while decorative details have varied. Buildings are typically bilaterally symmetrical, arranged around enclosed courtyards, and oriented horizontally. Their form varies by rank and purpose, from [[Palace|palaces]] such as the [[Forbidden City]] to [[Pagoda|pagodas]]. Starting with the [[Tang dynasty]], the style strongly influenced architecture in Japan, Korea, Vietnam, and Mongolia. Since the 20th century, urban development has favored high-rises over traditional buildings, which are normally less than three levels, while traditional carpentry and masonry continue in rural vernacular architecture.

Visual art originating in China, Greater China, or practiced by Chinese artists. Major forms include [[Calligraphy|calligraphy]], painting, [[Sculpture|sculpture]], [[Architecture|architecture]], [[Garden|garden]] design, [[Porcelain|porcelain]], bronze work, lacquerware, and textiles. Chinese art strongly influenced the arts of Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, and imported porcelain, lacquer, and silk prompted imitations in Europe. Much of the finest work, especially ceramics, was produced in imperial and large workshop factories by largely unknown artists. Ink wash painting, practiced mainly by scholar-officials, developed aesthetic values similar to those of the West. After 1949, Socialist Realism became the dominant officially sanctioned style, and the [[Cultural Revolution]] (1966–1976) saw much of the artistic heritage suppressed or destroyed. Since the 1980s, traditional forms have been revived and avant-garde movements have emerged.

Lunisolar calendar used by the Chinese people. Its twelve months are aligned with the phases of the moon, with an intercalary month added as needed to keep the calendar in step with the seasons, and each month has 29 or 30 days. It also has 24 solar terms, and the winter solstice must occur in the eleventh month. A total of 102 calendars have been officially recorded in classical texts, and results vary by location, so calculations for [[Beijing]] and [[Nanjing]] can differ. Originating in the [[Shang dynasty]] as the Yin calendar, it still fixes the date of [[Chinese New Year]] and is linked to the [[Chinese zodiac]]. Modern China officially uses the [[Gregorian calendar]].

Logographic writing system used for the Chinese languages and, historically, for others influenced by Chinese culture. Chinese characters generally represent morphemes, units of meaning, rather than sounds. They are one of four independently invented writing systems accepted by scholars, and the only one still in continuous use. The earliest attested characters are oracle bone inscriptions from the 13th century BCE, made for divinations by the [[Shang dynasty]] in present-day Anyang, [[Henan]]. Clerical script, matured by the [[Han dynasty]], abstracted the forms of characters. Writing everyday vocabulary requires roughly 2,000 to 3,000 characters. Simplified characters are used in mainland China, Singapore, and Malaysia, and traditional characters in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau. In Japanese they are called [[Kanji|kanji]], and more than 100,000 characters have been included in the [[Unicode]] Standard.

Culinary traditions originating in China and among Chinese communities abroad. Cuisine varies with geography, from the tropical south to the subarctic northeast, and with social class and religion. Northern dishes rely on wheat, millet, noodles, and bread, while rice was cultivated in the south. Restaurants in the modern sense emerged in [[Song dynasty]] China in the 11th and 12th centuries. A 1980 grouping of the Eight Cuisines of China named Anhui, Guangdong, Fujian, Hunan, Jiangsu, Shandong, Sichuan, and [[Zhejiang]]. Chinese food is intertwined with [[Traditional Chinese medicine|traditional Chinese medicine]], and staples such as [[Soy sauce|soy sauce]], [[Tofu|tofu]], and tea are now found worldwide. Cooks judge a dish by its ingredients, knife work, cooking time, and seasoning.

One of the world's oldest and most extensive literary traditions. It begins with the earliest recorded inscriptions and court archives and includes major works of philosophy and history from the Axial Age, mostly written in [[Classical Chinese]]. The Confucian Four Books and Five Classics became the basis of the imperial examinations in the 12th century. The [[Tang dynasty|Han and Tang dynasties]] were golden ages of poetry, with [[Li Bai]] and [[Du Fu]] among the best known. Ming and Qing writers produced mature novels such as *Dream of the Red Chamber*, written in vernacular Chinese. The early 20th-century vernacular movement made [[Lu Xun]] an influential voice. In the People's Republic era, literature has operated under state oversight, and critics argue that censorship has constrained writers and limited depictions of events such as the [[Great Leap Forward]] famines.

Fighting styles developed over centuries in China, commonly called kung fu or wushu. Styles are classified as internal (*neijia*), focusing on [[Qi|qi]] manipulation, or external (*waijia*), building muscle and cardiovascular fitness; northern and southern traditions form another classification. Legend credits the [[Yellow Emperor]] with the earliest fighting systems, and the *Spring and Autumn Annals* (5th century BC) mention a hand-to-hand combat theory. Since the 1950s the People's Republic has organized the art as an exhibition and full-contact sport called wushu. Debate continues over combat effectiveness: some studies report benefits such as improved balance, while critics note that traditional forms have shown little advantage in mixed-rules fights.

Body of myths passed down orally and in literature throughout Greater China. Creation myths include Pangu creating the world from his body and Nuwa mending the sky. Culture heroes are credited with teaching skills ranging from building houses to writing, and some are revered as ancestors of ethnic groups or dynasties, such as the [[Yellow Emperor]]. Like many mythologies, it was once regarded at least partly as a factual record of the past. Mythology forms part of [[Chinese folk religion]] and of religious [[Taoism]], and it is intertwined with the concepts of li and [[Qi|qi]]. Literary tales include *Journey to the West*.

Philosophical traditions of China, spanning more than two millennia. Philosophy began in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, known as the "Hundred Schools of Thought", when [[Confucius]], [[Mencius]], and [[Laozi]] laid foundations for [[Confucianism]], [[Taoism]], Mohism, and [[Legalism (Chinese philosophy)|Legalism]]. Confucianism became the official ideology under the Han dynasty. Later, Indian [[Buddhism]] influenced Chinese thought, and [[Zhu Xi]] helped systematize Neo-Confucianism in the Song and Ming dynasties. In the modern era, Chinese thinkers engaged with Western thought, producing Chinese Marxism and New Confucianism. Confucianism emphasizes ethical cultivation and political responsibility, while Daoism advocates living in accordance with nature.

Scheme assigning an animal to each year in a repeating twelve-year cycle. The animals are the Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, and Pig. The system was standardized in the [[Han dynasty]], when it was combined with ten Heavenly Stems to form a 60-year cycle. According to legend, the [[Jade Emperor]] held a race to choose the animals. The zodiac is popular across [[East Asia]], [[Central Asia]], and Southeast Asia, where people believe that the animal of a person's birth year influences personality, career, and compatibility.

Soviet and Kyrgyz author and diplomat who wrote mainly in Russian, and also in Kyrgyz. He is one of the best-known figures in Kyrgyz literature. Born in Sheker to a Kyrgyz father and Tatar mother, he saw his father charged with "bourgeois nationalism" in 1937 and executed in 1938. After studying at the Maxim Gorky Literature Institute in [[Moscow]], he worked for Pravda for eight years and joined the Communist Party of the [[Soviet Union]] in 1959. He endorsed the glasnost policies of [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] and later became a diplomat and adviser to him. His novel *Jamila* (1958) brought him international attention, and later works such as *The Day Lasts More Than a Hundred Years* (1980) drew on folklore.

Nigerian novelist, poet, and critic regarded as a central figure of modern African literature. Born in Ogidi in colonial Nigeria, he drew on [[Igbo people|Igbo]] traditions and Christian influences, and defended writing in English as a means to reach a broad audience. His first novel, *Things Fall Apart* (1958), is the most widely studied and translated African novel. With *No Longer at Ease* (1960) and *Arrow of God* (1964) it forms the "African Trilogy". His 1975 essay "An Image of Africa" criticized [[Joseph Conrad]]'s *Heart of Darkness* as racist, though some critics argue that it overlooked Conrad's anti-imperial intent. He supported Biafran independence during the [[Nigerian Civil War]] and later taught in the United States, at Bard College and [[Brown University]]. He rejected the label "father of modern African literature".

Small, striped burrowing [[Squirrel|squirrels]] of the subtribe Tamiina. Chipmunks live throughout [[North America]], except for the Siberian chipmunk, which is found mainly in [[Asia]]. The 25 living species are omnivorous, eating seeds, [[Nut (fruit)|nuts]], fruits, buds, and occasionally insects. They carry food in their cheek pouches to store in burrows for winter, and this storage helps disperse seedlings and fungi in [[Forest|forests]]. Chipmunks are considered pests in some areas, where they eat grains and vegetables grown by humans.
